A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Collab-Overcooked. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support comparison, including material retained under different numbering or placement.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 10 LLMs, experiments with 10 human participants, and task-decomposition, positional-dependence, and time-limit analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds DeepSeek-R1 evaluations, timed human experiments, attention-distribution analyses, and attention-intervention outcomes.

M1.justification: Section 5.3.4 adds an experimental inference variant that manually reallocates attention toward patterns observed in successful cases before regenerating outputs. The standard agent architecture, communication, memory/reflection mechanisms, and benchmark scoring remain intact. Attention-guided fine-tuning remains future work.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same 30 cooking tasks across six complexity levels in the same two-agent, resource-isolated environment. The added attention experiments use existing task levels. Human timing and communication changes concern procedures within retained task coverage; renamed recipe examples do not establish new tasks.

E2.justification: DeepSeek-R1 joins the evaluated models in Table 2 and Figure 3, with all 10 earlier models retained. In the human comparison, Figure 4 replaces GPT-4o with DeepSeek-R1. Moving Qwen2.5-32B between Figure 3 panels is regrouping rather than comparator removal.

E3.justification: Appendix C.2 introduces 10-, 15-, and 20-second human decision limits, permits verbal communication, and excludes subsequent action entry from timing. New attention experiments compare successful and failed outputs and regenerate outputs under attention intervention with model parameters held fixed. The main benchmark retains its metrics, gamma of 1.5, and beta of 0.95.

E4.justification: v2 adds a substantial investigation of attention allocation and collaboration failures, including correlations and interventions for Qwen2.5-7B and 72B at Levels 1 and 5. It also adds human time-pressure sensitivity results. The earlier decomposition, positional-dependence, error analyses, and case studies are retained, principally in Appendices C.4–C.5.

E5.justification: Figure 12 introduces attention-distribution boxplots and Pearson correlation tests with p-values, adding formal statistical analysis absent from v1. Section 5.3.4 newly reports matching random seeds for intervention comparisons. The retained experiments still specify 10 repetitions per task and 20 trials per selected scenario; an increase in those run counts is not reported.

E6.justification: All 10 original Table 2 rows remain numerically unchanged. Added DeepSeek-R1 results include success rates of 82%, 44%, and 30% at Levels 4–6, with reported token usage 18.6 times GPT-4o's. v2 also adds recipe statistics, timed human results, attention correlations, and intervention outcomes correcting 35–64% of previously incorrect cases. The revised human results use changed conditions.

T1.justification: The TES, ITES, PC, IC, and RC formulas and RAT assumptions retain their mathematical substance. Trajectory notation is rewritten, and Appendix B.2 adds interpretation of IC and RC, without introducing a new definition, derivation, theorem, or proof.

C1.justification: The benchmark and process-oriented evaluation contributions remain, but the introduction and conclusion shift the central diagnosis from maintaining collaboration performance to attention misalignment. v2 makes attention analysis an explicit contribution and claims that correcting attention alone improves collaboration, substantially expanding the paper's principal scientific claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds causal interpretations involving attention to recipes, collaboration rules, environmental observations, and partner instructions. It attributes human advantages to procedural abstraction versus shallow agent memory, adds a rationale for the two-agent design, and develops collaborative-memory and attention-guided training recommendations. The original limitations concerning RAT enumeration, evaluation cost, and simple baselines remain.

D1.justification: Appendix C.3 documents prompt segmentation and first-generated-token attention aggregation; C.2 adds detailed human timing rules. Some retained documentation becomes less specific: Figure 7 changes 'Latest 5' memory to 'Latest K', and Listing 6 replaces the rotated recipe with an unreordered example despite retaining the rotation description. These edits do not establish corresponding changes to the underlying retained experiments.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for DeepSeek-R1 and GPT models, plus Li et al. (2023b, 2024a) to contextualize collaboration and instruction-tracking difficulties. Section 5.3.4 adds a targeted novelty claim about attention-driven failures under information and resource isolation. The existing related-work taxonomy and benchmark comparison in Table 1 remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The human-performance discussion, failure-analysis narrative, future directions, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. The former three-part main-text failure analysis is compressed and consolidated with expanded, descriptively named Appendix C.4 subsections. Appendix B.2 and an Ethics Statement are added, alongside smaller language and author-list edits.

P2.justification: v2 adds attention-intervention charts, a prompt-segmentation diagram, attention-distribution boxplots, and recipe-statistics and human-timing tables. Figure 3 changes model groupings and expands its vertical scales to 100%; Figure 4 is redrawn for the revised comparison. The original Figure 5 is retained intact as appendix Figure 9, substantially reorganizing the visual evidence.

improvement.justification: DeepSeek-R1 supplies a more demanding model reference with an explicit token-cost tradeoff, while timed human evaluations test the robustness of the human advantage. Attention analyses add useful diagnostic evidence. However, strong causal claims lack sufficiently specified intervention details, new collaboration counts conflict between Tables 3 and 4, and Listing 6 no longer illustrates the claimed reordering. These documentation and interpretation weaknesses limit the overall gain.
